title: Councils can manage street parking with permits and pricing, independently of what new buildings provide
oneLiner: Kerbside space is the council's to allocate; it does not have to be first-come, first-served.
body: Resident permit schemes, time limits and paid parking are standard tools and are already used in most inner suburbs. They address street crowding directly, whatever the parking provision in new buildings, and can be introduced in the same decision that removes the minimum.
contextBackground: This is the standard answer to the spillover objection and is the usual companion measure where minimums have been removed.
contextDisagreement: The tools exist and work. The disagreement is political: residents who currently park free on the street are being asked to accept permits or charges so that new residents can pay less for housing.

otherClaim.title: Without minimums, residents' cars spill onto surrounding streets and crowd out existing residents

claimItself.title: Without minimums, residents' cars spill onto surrounding streets and crowd out existing residents
claimItself.oneLiner: If the building does not house the cars, the street does.
claimItself.body: Residents of new developments will own cars at roughly the rate of their neighbours, whatever the building provides. Opponents of removal argue the predictable result is competition for kerbside space that existing residents regard as theirs.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Up to 40 per cent of residential and on-street parking in inner Melbourne sits empty at night, and most street spaces are used by residents who already have off-street parking
